title: Kesswil to Küsnacht: The Way of the Stone
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Kesswil, the parsonage on Lake Constance
stops.campa: In the parsonage at Kesswil, on the flat shore of Lake Constance, the pastor's wife Emilie Preiswerk bears a son to Johann Paul Achilles Jung. The child is named Carl Gustav after his grandfather, the Basel physician whom the city holds to be a natural son of Goethe: the legend the family carries like a sealed letter. The lake lies enormous before the house; his first memory will be of sun glittering through leaves, and of that inconceivable water. The House of Jung receives its rememberer.

stops.name: Schloss Laufen, the parsonage above the Rhine Falls
stops.campa: The family moves to the castle-parsonage of Laufen, perched directly over the Rhine falls. The cataract roars day and night beneath the child's window. Fishermen drown in the river; corpses are recovered on the rocks; black-coated men carry long boxes into the churchyard while his father speaks in a resounding voice at the graveside. The boy learns that Lord Jesus takes people to himself, and begins to distrust the taking. The falls become the ground-bass of his childhood, the sound under everything.

stops.name: Laufen, the underground temple and the man-eater
stops.campa: Aged between three and four, the boy dreams the first great dream of his life. In the meadow by the vicarage a stone-lined hole opens; a stair leads down to a doorway hung with green brocade. Beyond it, a red carpet runs to a golden throne, and on the throne stands an enormous phallus of naked flesh, twelve or fifteen feet high, a single eye gazing motionless upward from its rounded head. His mother's voice cries out above him in the dark. The subterranean god has shown himself first; the dream will haunt him for fifty years.
stops.quote: Yes, just look at him. That is the man-eater!
stops.quote_source: Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 1 (the mother's voice in the dream)

stops.name: Klein-Hüningen, the parsonage by the Rhine
stops.campa: Pastor Jung is called to Klein-Hüningen, the fishing village at Basel's edge where the Wiese meets the Rhine. The family occupies the eighteenth-century parsonage with its great garden, its washhouse, its attic. Here the boy grows among peasant children, barges, floods, and the bones of the village churchyard. His mother by day is kindly and stout; by night, he perceives, she is uncanny: a priestess of the bear-cave, speaking with a second voice that says true things. The two atmospheres of his life, day and night, take up residence.

stops.name: Klein-Hüningen, the fire in the stones
stops.campa: In the garden wall before the parsonage the boy keeps a fire burning in a cave of the old stones: a fire that must burn forever, which he alone may tend; other children may feed only profane fires. Nearby juts his stone, the slope-set block on which he sits for hours playing the game of the exchanged question: he is sitting on the stone, but the stone may equally be saying 'he' of him. Thirty years later the question will be answered in masonry at Bollingen. The stone has already claimed him.
stops.quote: Am I the one who is sitting on the stone, or am I the stone on which he is sitting?

stops.name: Klein-Hüningen, the manikin in the attic beam
stops.campa: Toward the end of his tenth year the boy carves a little man with frock coat, top hat and shining boots, saws him from his ruler, and lays him in the pencil-case on a bed of wool with a smooth black Rhine stone painted into upper and lower halves: the manikin's own stone. He hides the case on the forbidden beam in the attic and visits it in secret, slipping in tiny scrolls written in a private script. No one can discover it; no one can destroy it. It is the first secret, the first god in the roof, and the torment of being divided against himself is gone.
stops.quote: The possession of a secret had a very powerful formative influence on my character; I consider it the essential factor of my boyhood.

stops.name: Basel, the Gymnasium am Münsterplatz
stops.campa: The country pastor's son walks daily into Basel to the Gymnasium beside the cathedral, among the sons of patricians who ride in carriages and speak of the Alps and the sea. For the first time he knows that his family is poor, that his boots are broken. Yet he carries the other knowledge too: that within him lives a second personality, an old man of the eighteenth century, buckled shoes and white wig, dignified and near to God, beside the schoolboy. Number One and Number Two begin their long negotiation on this square.

stops.name: Basel Münster, the cathedral vision
stops.campa: On a fine summer day the boy comes out of school onto the square and sees the cathedral roof glittering, new-tiled, under a blue sky, and thinks: the world is beautiful, and God made it and sits above it on a golden throne, and there the thought chokes. For three days and two nights he fights the forbidden conclusion, certain it means eternal damnation. Then he understands that God himself demands the sin of thinking it, as He demanded disobedience of Adam, and he lets the thought come. Grace descends on the Münsterplatz like weather. He has thought God to the end and lived.
stops.quote: God sits on His golden throne, high above the world — and from under the throne an enormous turd falls upon the sparkling new roof, shatters it, and breaks the walls of the cathedral asunder.

stops.name: Basel, the fainting spells conquered
stops.campa: A boy knocks him down on the cathedral square; his head strikes a curbstone. In the half-second of falling comes the thought: now you won't have to go to school any more. For six months the fainting spells excuse him from lessons, until he overhears his father confide to a visitor that the doctors fear epilepsy, that the boy may never earn his living. Struck as by lightning, he goes to his father's study, takes up his Latin grammar, and faints three times over it, and works on through each attack until the spells never return. He has met the neurosis and learned what it is.
stops.quote: Why, then, I must get to work!

stops.name: University of Basel, matriculation
stops.campa: Jung matriculates in medicine at the University of Basel, where his grandfather Carl Gustav the elder, Goethe's son, as Basel whispers and this register affirms, once held the chair and rebuilt the anatomy. In the Zofingia fraternity the young man lectures on the border zones of exact science, on the soul as something real, scandalous among materialists. Nietzsche's ghost still walks these streets and Bachofen in the flesh; Jung reads Kant, Schopenhauer, and the spiritualists by night. The grandfather's double inheritance, scalpel and Faust, is taken up.

stops.name: Basel, the séances with Helene Preiswerk
stops.campa: In the Preiswerk household his fifteen-year-old cousin Helly falls into trance at the table. Dead grandfather Samuel Preiswerk, the Hebraist who kept a chair for the spirits, speaks through her; she becomes Ivenes, a wise woman who travels among the stars and unrolls the family's past lives. For four years Jung attends the Saturday sittings, recording everything: the somnambulisms, the invented cosmology drawn in circles, the splinter-personalities forming and dissolving. Around the table the psyche shows him plainly that it is not one but many, and that the many want to become one.
sources: On the Psychology and Pathology of So-Called Occult Phenomena (1902)

stops.name: Basel, the father dies
stops.campa: Pastor Paul Jung dies in the Klein-Hüningen parsonage, broken on the faith he could not feel, having told his son only: believe, do not think. Carl, twenty, holds the dying man's head. Afterwards his mother speaks with her night voice, the second voice that is never wrong. The son inherits the unfinished religious question as other men inherit debts, and will pay on it for sixty-five years, down to a book called Answer to Job. The family moves; Carl becomes head of the house on a subsistence of borrowed francs and fossil-selling.
stops.quote: He died in time for you.
stops.quote_source: Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 3 (the mother's No. 2 voice)

stops.name: Basel, Krafft-Ebing read: the flash of illumination
stops.campa: Preparing for his state examinations, Jung opens Krafft-Ebing's textbook of psychiatry, the despised specialty, and reads that the psychoses are diseases of the personality. His heart pounds; he must stand up and draw breath. In one stroke the two rivers of his life, nature and spirit, biology and the séance table, flow into a single bed. His teachers are dismayed: he is throwing away a career in internal medicine for the back ward. He knows, with the certainty of vocation, that the collision of nature and spirit has become fact in him.
stops.quote: Here alone the two currents of my interest could flow together and in a united stream dig their own bed.

stops.name: Burghölzli asylum, Zurich: the entry into the monastery of the mad
stops.campa: On 10 December 1900 Jung passes the gates of the Burghölzli, the cantonal asylum on its hill above Zurich, as assistant to Eugen Bleuler. He does not leave the grounds for six months; he reads fifty volumes of the Allgemeine Zeitschrift für Psychiatrie from the beginning, to learn how the psychiatric mind thinks. The Basel world of Bachofen and legend is behind him; here is the monastic world of ward rounds at dawn, abstinence, and the uncanny speech of the insane, which he alone suspects of meaning something.
stops.quote: With my work at Burghölzli, life took on an undivided reality — all intention, consciousness, duty, and responsibility.

stops.name: Neuhausen am Rheinfall, the wedding above the falls
stops.campa: Jung marries Emma Rauschenbach of Schaffhausen, daughter of the industrialist, whom he first saw on a staircase when she was fourteen and knew at once for his wife. The civil ceremony is held on 14 February; the wedding ball glitters that night at the Hotel Bellevue in Neuhausen, directly above the Rhine falls: the same cataract that thundered under his cradle at Laufen. Two days later the church bells of the Steigkirche confirm it. The circle by the falls closes; the foundation of the house is laid.

stops.name: Burghölzli, the word-association experiments
stops.campa: With stopwatch and galvanometer Jung reads a hundred words to patients and clerks and measures the hesitations. Where the reaction stumbles, something answers that is not the conscious man: a knot of feeling-charged images, autonomous, defended. He names it the complex, and the word enters every language on earth. His 1902 dissertation had already treated cousin Helly's spirits as psychology; now the laboratory confirms the séance. The apparatus detects a thief among the nurses; the invisible interior has become measurable, and Vienna will soon take notice.

stops.name: Burghölzli, the secrets of the mad heard
stops.campa: Against all doctrine Jung listens to the content of psychosis. Old Babette, mocked as burnt-out, proves to be guarding a wounded royalty: 'I am the Lorelei; I am Socrates' deputy', dream-logic defending her dignity. A young woman entrusts him with her secret: she has lived on the moon, where she fought the vampire who steals women, and does not wish to return to a shabby earth. He receives the secret orders of the mad as dispatches from a real country. The psychosis contains a meaning: on this heresy his whole science will be built.
stops.quote: At bottom we discover nothing new and unknown in the mentally ill; rather, we encounter the substratum of our own natures.

stops.name: Burghölzli, the correspondence with Vienna opens
stops.campa: Jung sends his Diagnostic Association Studies to Sigmund Freud in Vienna, whose Interpretation of Dreams he has defended before hostile congresses at the cost of his own respectability. Freud answers by return post, warm as a hand extended across the Reich. Letter follows letter through the year, the older man courting, the younger burning. Bleuler's whole Zurich clinic swings behind psychoanalysis: the first university foothold Freud has ever had. The two greatest map-makers of the interior have found each other; the meeting is now only a matter of a train.

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19, the thirteen hours
stops.campa: Jung climbs the stairs of Berggasse 19 at one o'clock in the afternoon and the two men talk, virtually without pause, for thirteen hours. Freud, fifty, precise, ironic, the first man of real importance Jung has met; Jung, thirty-one, torrential, bringing the asylum and the séance room in his luggage. Freud marks him that week as son and heir: the crown prince who will carry psychoanalysis out of the Jewish quarter into the world. Only on the sexual theory does something in Jung reserve itself, quietly, like a stone in a field waiting.
stops.quote: We met at one o'clock in the afternoon and talked virtually without a pause for thirteen hours. Freud was the first man of real importance I had encountered.

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19, the bookcase speaks
stops.campa: On the second visit, in Freud's study at evening, Jung asks the master's view of precognition and psychokinesis and is answered with shallow positivism. A curious sensation rises in Jung, his diaphragm grown iron and red-hot, and a detonation cracks out of the bookcase beside them, so loud both men start up. Jung declares it a catalytic exteriorization phenomenon; Freud calls it bosh; Jung prophesies a second report, and the bookcase cracks again on his word. Freud stares aghast. The spirits have voted in the master's own furniture, and the master has abstained.
stops.quote: 'There, that is an example of a so-called catalytic exteriorization phenomenon.' 'Oh come,' he exclaimed. 'That is sheer bosh.' 'It is not... and to prove my point I now predict that in a moment there will be another such loud report!' Sure enough, no sooner had I said the words than the same detonation went off in the bookcase.
suggested_refs: Freud's letter to Jung on the 'poltergeist' (16 April 1909)

stops.name: Küsnacht, the house built on the lake
stops.campa: Jung leaves the Burghölzli and moves his family into the great yellow house he has built at Seestrasse 228, Küsnacht, garden running down to the water of Lake Zurich. Over the stone door he has carved the oracle the Spartans received before Delphi's god, found in Erasmus: called or not called, the god will be present. Every patient, postman and prince who enters for the next fifty-two years passes under that sentence. The house is ship and temple at once; here the work will be done, and here he will die.
stops.quote: VOCATUS ATQUE NON VOCATUS DEUS ADERIT
stops.quote_source: Inscription carved over the door at Seestrasse 228, Küsnacht

stops.name: Bremen, Freud faints at the peat-bog dead
stops.campa: Freud, Jung and Ferenczi gather at Bremen to sail for America. At luncheon Jung, full of the north, talks on and on about the peat-bog corpses: the prehistoric dead of the moors, tanned whole by the brown water, ploughed up like sleeping men. Freud grows irritable: why do you care so much about corpses? Then he falls from his chair in a dead faint. Recovering, he confesses his conviction that the talk of the dead means Jung harbours a death-wish against him. Over the harbour the omen hangs plainly: the father has seen his own barrow.
sources: Ernest Jones, Life and Work of Sigmund Freud

stops.name: At sea aboard the George Washington, the house of many floors
stops.campa: Seven days on the Atlantic, and the three analysts analyze each other's dreams on deck. Jung dreams the decisive one: his own house, upper storey rococo and inhabited, and below it a sixteenth-century floor, and below that a Roman cellar, and beneath the cellar a low cave cut in rock where scattered bones and broken pottery lie in thick dust: two human skulls, very old, half disintegrated. Freud, following him down floor by floor, sticks fast at the skulls and asks whose death Jung wishes. But Jung has seen the true architecture: beneath the personal psyche, the immemorial floors of mankind.
stops.quote: It was plain to me that the house represented a kind of image of the psyche — that is to say, of my then state of consciousness, with hitherto unconscious additions.
suggested_refs: The dream of the house (MDR ch. 5)

stops.name: Clark University, Worcester, the New World crowned
stops.campa: At Clark University's vigentennial, Freud and Jung lecture to the assembled sages of America, William James among them, who walks apart with Jung and speaks openly of psychical research and the varieties of religious experience. Jung presents the association experiments; honorary doctorates descend on both travelers on 10 September. Psychoanalysis, scandal of Vienna, is suddenly academic, transatlantic, inevitable. In the group photograph on the steps the whole apostolic generation stands together once, and never again.
suggested_refs: Clark 1909 group photograph (Freud, Jung, James, Hall)

stops.name: Nuremberg, president of the new church
stops.campa: At the second Psychoanalytic Congress the International Psychoanalytical Association is founded and Freud drives through Jung's election as president: the gentile heir who will save the doctrine from being a Jewish national affair. The Viennese revolt in a hotel room; Freud pleads that they are all in danger. To Jung privately he has already spoken the fatal sentence of dogma: promise me never to abandon the sexual theory, we must make of it a bulwark: against the black tide of mud, of occultism. In that word 'bulwark' Jung hears a church door closing, with himself inside.
stops.quote: My dear Jung, promise me never to abandon the sexual theory. That is the most essential thing of all... we must make a dogma of it, an unshakable bulwark... against the black tide of mud — of occultism.
stops.quote_source: Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 5 (Freud's words as Jung records them)

stops.name: Weimar, the congress in Goethe's town
stops.campa: The third congress convenes at Weimar, in the town of Goethe: the ancestor of the legend, whose atlas the corpus keeps. Emma Jung attends; so do the first women analysts, Lou Andreas-Salomé among them, ranged in the famous photograph before the men. Jung, president, is at zenith: tall, laughing, the movement's future. Yet he is already deep in the night-sea of Miss Miller's fantasies, writing the book on libido whose second half he knows will cost him everything. In Goethe's town, Goethe's descendant prepares his own Faustian breach.

stops.name: Küsnacht, Wandlungen: the sacrifice prepared
stops.campa: Part two of Wandlungen und Symbole der Libido is published: the libido widened from sexuality into the energy of life itself, the hero's incest read as return to the mother of rebirth, not lust. For two months Jung could not touch the chapter called 'The Sacrifice,' knowing what its printing would sacrifice. Emma tells him: write it. In New York that autumn he says it aloud at Fordham. The book is his own hero-making and his own parricide; Freud reads it and the temperature of the letters begins to fall toward silence.
stops.quote: For two months I was unable to touch my pen, so tormented was I by the conflict.

stops.name: Munich, Park Hotel, Freud faints in Jung's arms
stops.campa: At a conference of presidents in the Park Hotel the two men patch their quarrel over lunch, and the talk turns to Amenhotep IV, who struck his father's name from the monuments to found the religion of the sun. Freud insists the erasure is the essence; Jung answers that Amenhotep was a creator, not a parricide. Freud slides from his chair in a faint. Jung gathers him up like a child and carries him to a couch; half-waking, Freud murmurs of the sweetness of dying. The father has fainted twice now at the same ghost, and both men know its name.
stops.quote: How sweet it must be to die.
stops.quote_source: Freud's words on waking, as recorded in Jung's account and Jones's Life and Work
sources: Ernest Jones, Life and Work of Sigmund Freud

stops.name: Küsnacht, the letters end
stops.campa: After Jung's scalding December letter (I shall point out your neurosis to you since you deal out diagnoses like a pope), Freud proposes that they abandon personal relations entirely. From Küsnacht, on 6 January 1913, Jung writes the reply that seals it, borrowing Hamlet's dying words for the grave of the greatest friendship psychology will ever waste. Six years of letters, near six hundred of them, fall silent. The crown prince is disinherited and free, and the freedom opens directly downward, into the flood he does not yet know is coming.
stops.quote: I accede to your wish that we abandon our personal relations, for I never thrust my friendship on anyone... 'The rest is silence.'
stops.quote_source: Jung to Freud, 6 January 1913, The Freud/Jung Letters

stops.name: Munich, the last sight of Freud
stops.campa: At the fourth congress in Munich the movement splits down the middle of the hall. Jung is re-elected president, but twenty-two abstain in cold protest; Lou Andreas-Salomé notes his forced gaiety. He and Freud pass one another without words. In the corridors Jung speaks for the first time of psychological types, that Freud's truth and Adler's truth are truths of two different natures, the doctrine that will make peace possible only after the war is total. The two men part on the pavement and never see each other again in this world.

stops.name: The train at Schaffhausen, Europe drowned in blood
stops.campa: Riding alone toward Schaffhausen in October, Jung is seized while awake. A monstrous flood covers the northern lands between the North Sea and the Alps; he sees the yellow waves, the floating rubble of civilization, the drowned bodies of uncounted thousands, and then the whole sea turns to blood, lapping to the foot of the mountains that guard Switzerland. The vision holds him one hour, to the point of nausea. Two weeks later it returns with a voice: look at it well, it is wholly real, it will be so. He concludes he is menaced by psychosis; the year 1914 will read the diagnosis differently.
stops.quote: I saw the mighty yellow waves, the floating rubble of civilization, and the drowned bodies of uncounted thousands. Then the whole sea turned to blood.
suggested_refs: Red Book, Liber Primus opening visions

stops.name: Küsnacht, the plunge: 12 December 1913
stops.campa: Sitting at his desk in Küsnacht on the twelfth of December, having resolved to meet whatever rises, Jung lets himself drop. The ground gives way beneath his feet and he plunges into dark depths, landing in soft sticky mire at the mouth of a cave where a mummified dwarf guards the entrance and a red crystal glows above an underground stream. He wades in, lifts the stone, and the corpse of a blond hero floats past, followed by a black scarab and a red new-born sun; blood gushes from the opening. The descent has begun; he will keep this appointment nightly for six years, and the Black Books fill.
stops.quote: Then I let myself drop. Suddenly it was as though the ground literally gave way beneath my feet, and I plunged down into dark depths.

stops.name: Küsnacht, the killing of Siegfried
stops.campa: Six nights later Jung dreams he crouches with a brown savage in the rocks of a high mountain at dawn, and when Siegfried comes down the slope in a chariot of bones, radiant, they shoot him dead and the rain falls to wash out the traces. He wakes with a revolver in the drawer beside him and an inner voice pronouncing sentence: understand the dream or use the gun. He understands: the hero, the will, the shining Germanic ideal in himself, must die, and grief comes, and the rain. The secret of the dream is the first mercy of the descent.
stops.quote: If you do not understand the dream, you must shoot yourself!
stops.quote_source: Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 6 (the inner voice)
suggested_refs: Red Book, the Siegfried dream folio

stops.name: Küsnacht lakeshore, Philemon of the kingfisher wings
stops.campa: Out of the fantasies rises a figure who is not Jung: an old man with the horns of a bull, bearing four keys, borne on kingfisher wings across a sky sown with clods of earth: Philemon, pagan and Gnostic, lame of foot. Jung paints him; and while painting, walking his garden on the lakeshore, he finds a dead kingfisher, a bird all but unknown on Lake Zurich, unmarked, dead two or three days at most. The lake has countersigned the vision. Philemon becomes his teacher, walking the garden with him, saying: you do not make your thoughts; they are like animals in a forest, or people in a room.
stops.quote: Philemon and other figures of my fantasies brought home to me the crucial insight that there are things in the psyche which I do not produce, but which produce themselves and have their own life.

stops.name: Aberdeen, the war answers the visions
stops.campa: Jung is in Aberdeen addressing the British Medical Association on the importance of the unconscious in psychopathology when the lamps of Europe go out. On the first of August the world war breaks: the flood, the sea of blood, the frozen summer of his three spring dreams stand revealed as no private madness but the continent's own dream, seen early from a Swiss train. His personal fate and the fate of mankind are welded in one piece. He makes his way home through a mobilizing world, and his task stands before him, clear.
stops.quote: Now my task was clear: I had to try to understand what had happened and to what extent my own experience coincided with that of mankind in general.

stops.name: Küsnacht, the dead return from Jerusalem: the Seven Sermons
stops.campa: On a Sunday afternoon the house at Küsnacht fills with presences. The front doorbell rings frantically with no one at the door: the maids see it move; the daughters have dreamed all week of ghosts; the son draws a fisherman he cannot explain; the air grows thick with spirit until Jung cries out: what in the world is this? And they answer in chorus the sentence that becomes the first line of the Septem Sermones ad Mortuos. Over three evenings Jung writes the sermons in the voice of Basilides of Alexandria, and as the ink dries the haunting lifts, the house breathes, the dead are answered.
stops.quote: We have come back from Jerusalem, where we found not what we sought.
stops.quote_source: Septem Sermones ad Mortuos; Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 6

stops.name: Château d'Oex, the commandant draws mandalas
stops.campa: Called up as commandant of the British interned soldiers at Château d'Oex in the Vaud Alps, Jung rises each morning and sketches in a notebook a small circular drawing, a mandala, which corresponds to his inner situation of that day, and watches the circles correct him, rebuke him, restore him. Here he grasps what the years of descent were seeking: the goal is not a line but a centre; the self is the circumference and the midpoint; all paths are circumambulations. The war ends around him while the commandant of the interned discovers the geometry of the soul.
stops.quote: I sketched every morning in a notebook a small circular drawing, a mandala, which seemed to correspond to my inner situation at the time.

stops.name: Algiers, Europe seen from outside
stops.campa: Jung lands at Algiers in the March light, his first step off the European shelf. The muezzin's cry, the white city stacked against the hill, the unhurried crowds: time itself runs at another pace here, and he feels the centuries fall away like coats. What Europe calls Oriental apathy he reads at once as a different relation of the ego to the sun. He has come, he realizes, not to study the Arab but to catch sight of the European, himself, from a point outside, and the sight is not flattering.

stops.name: Tunis, the older time
stops.campa: In the medina of Tunis Jung walks for hours without a plan, letting the souks close over him. Here is a civilization layered like his Atlantic dream-house: French officialdom on top, then the Ottoman, the Arab, the Roman, Carthage under everything and the desert under Carthage. He feels the emotional tug of this world on some stratum of himself that Europe has paved over, and feels too a subtle danger, as of a man leaning over dark water. The unconscious, he notes, takes the features of whatever older world one enters.

stops.name: Sousse, the dream of the Arab prince
stops.campa: At Sousse, within the walls above the harbour, the answering dream comes. A young Arab prince, proud and handsome, attacks Jung on a bridge before a casbah, wrestles him, and tries to force his head under the water, to drown him, not quite to kill him, and then, in a vaulted chamber, is made to read Jung's own book. Waking, Jung understands: the dusky one is the shadow-royalty of his own soul, the self that Europe humiliates, which would rather drown the thinker than be unread. He carries the prince home with him, an ambassador accredited for life.

stops.name: Küsnacht, the mother dies; Wotan rides
stops.campa: Emilie Preiswerk-Jung dies suddenly in January. The night before the news reaches him, Jung dreams he stands in a dense, dark wood among gigantic primeval trees, and hears a wolf-howl and the shattering call of Wotan's wild hunt sweeping the sky: the Hunter come to fetch a soul of his own kin. He travels home through the night, and grief runs in him side by side with an incomprehensible undertone of the marriage-dance of the dead. The night-mother of the parsonage, the two-voiced priestess, is gathered to the older god she always half served.

stops.name: Bollingen, the Tower begun with his own hands
stops.campa: Two months after his mother's death Jung begins to build at Bollingen, on the reed-fringed shore of the upper lake he loved as a student: land bought from the church of St. Meinrad, old cloister ground. He learns to split stone from the Bollingen quarrymen and lays courses with his own hands. Words and paper are not real enough: the tower is his confession of faith in stone, round like the maternal hearth, without electricity or pipe-water, where the dead of the family may come to the fire and the twentieth century must wait outside on the road.
stops.quote: Words and paper, however, did not seem real enough to me; something more was needed. I had to make a confession of faith in stone. That was the beginning of the 'Tower.'

segments.name: Travels: The Pueblo and the Mountain of God

stops.name: Taos Pueblo, Mountain Lake speaks
stops.campa: On the roof of the adobe town under Taos Mountain, in the thin January sun, Jung sits wrapped in a blanket beside Ochwiay Biano, Mountain Lake, of the sun-keeping people. The Pueblo man says the whites are always seeking, their faces cruel and furrowed, and that the Indians think them mad. Jung asks why mad. Because they say they think with their heads. And what do you think with? We think here, says Mountain Lake, touching his heart. For the first time in his life, Jung records, someone has drawn for him the portrait of the real white man, and it strikes like a spear.
stops.quote: 'We think that they are mad.' I asked him why he thought the whites were all mad. 'They say that they think with their heads,' he replied. 'Why of course. What do you think with?' I asked him in surprise. 'We think here,' he said, indicating his heart.

stops.name: Mombasa, landfall of the Bugishu Psychological Expedition
stops.campa: Having sailed from Southampton on 15 October with Baynes and Beckwith, joined on the boat by Ruth Bailey, foretold as the fourth, Jung lands at Mombasa, humid, half-Arab, hung with mangoes and old Portuguese guns. The expedition carries a name half in jest, the Bugishu Psychological Expedition, and a purpose wholly serious: to find the psyche before Europe touched it. They take the night train inland, and Africa begins to burn away the doctor of Küsnacht layer by layer, like the label off a bottle in the rain.

stops.name: The Uganda railway, the man on the rock: five thousand years home
stops.campa: At first light the train curves along a red cliff, and above the carriage, motionless on a jag of rock, stands a slim black figure leaning on a long spear, gazing down. Jung is transfixed by the most intense sentiment du déjà vu of his life: he knows this man; he has known this moment always; he is not arriving in a foreign land but returning, after five thousand years, to the country of his youth. The railway rattles on toward Nairobi carrying a European who has just remembered something older than Europe.
stops.quote: I had the feeling that I had already experienced this moment and had always known this world.

stops.name: Athi Plains, the man who completes creation
stops.campa: From a low hill on the Athi Plains outside Nairobi, Jung looks out over gigantic herds of gazelle, antelope, gnu, zebra and warthog grazing and moving like slow rivers to the horizon, in a stillness that is the eternal beginning, the world as it was before anyone knew it was a world. His companions fade from his sight. Here the cosmic meaning of consciousness is given to him whole: in an invisible act of creation, man puts the stamp of perfection on the world by knowing it. The unknowing world sinks; the knower stands; the second cosmogony is accomplished on a hill in Kenya.
stops.quote: There the cosmic meaning of consciousness became overwhelmingly clear to me... Man, I, in an invisible act of creation put the stamp of perfection on the world by giving it objective existence.

stops.name: Mount Elgon, among the Elgonyi
stops.campa: The expedition camps at 7,000 feet on the slopes of Mount Elgon, the extinct volcano on the Uganda border, among the Elgonyi in their kraals. Under an old chief's courtesy Jung holds palavers on dreams and learns a hard news: since the English came, the big dreams have ceased: the District Commissioner now knows the future that the medicine-man once dreamed. The laibon says it with tears in his eyes. Jung writes it down like a man recording the extinction of a species: the dreaming office of mankind, resigning.

stops.name: Mount Elgon, the dawn worship: adhista
stops.campa: Each morning Jung leaves his tent to watch the sun come up over the Elgon forests, when the light unfolds like a polyphony and the world becomes for an instant so glorious that it hurts. The Elgonyi show him their only rite: at the moment the sun rises they spit on their hands and hold the palms to the first light, or breathe on them: offering to the risen god the living substance of the soul. Not the sun itself is God, the elders agree, but the moment of its rising: adhista. Jung recognizes the oldest prayer of mankind, and joins it privately for the rest of his life.
stops.quote: The sunrise in these latitudes was a phenomenon that overwhelmed me anew every day.

stops.name: Jinja, Ripon Falls, down the Nile
stops.campa: Striking camp after the turn of the year, the party crosses into Uganda and comes to Jinja, where the Nile pours out of Lake Victoria over the Ripon Falls and begins its four-thousand-mile argument with the desert. They embark northward with a paddle-steamer and a narrow-gauge patience, through Sudd and heat, Jung feverless and watchful, riding the river that runs like time itself from the lake-heart of Africa toward the tombs. He has chosen to leave Africa by the oldest road in the world, stern first, facing the interior.

stops.name: Aswan, Egypt entered from the south
stops.campa: By Khartoum and the desert rail the travelers descend into Egypt not as tourists from the Mediterranean but from within, from the south, from the source: the direction of the Nile itself and of the black Hamitic root under the pharaonic tree. At Aswan the granite islands stand in the brown water; northward wait the temples, where Jung reads the Horus-cry to the rising sun as the elder brother of the Elgonyi's spittle-offering. Africa closes behind him like a book whose sentence he was: the light is completed by the one who beholds it.

stops.name: Küsnacht, the Golden Flower arrives from Wilhelm
stops.campa: Jung paints a mandala with a golden castle at its centre and is troubled by its Chinese air: the forms, the colors, nothing European in it. As the paint dries, the post brings a package from Richard Wilhelm in Frankfurt: the manuscript of a thousand-year-old Taoist alchemical treatise, The Secret of the Golden Flower, with the request that he write a commentary. The coincidence breaks the isolation of a decade: his inner geometry has correspondents across the world and back through the centuries. He writes the word for it under the painting, and the word is synchronicity; and the road into alchemy stands open.
stops.quote: In remembrance of this coincidence, this 'synchronicity,' I wrote underneath the picture: 'In 1928, when I was painting this picture, showing the golden, well-fortified castle, Richard Wilhelm in Frankfurt sent me the thousand-year-old Chinese text on the yellow castle, the germ of the immortal body.'
suggested_refs: The Secret of the Golden Flower (1929)

stops.name: Zurich, Psychology Club, the Kundalini seminar
stops.campa: In the Psychology Club at Gemeindestrasse 27, following the indologist Wilhelm Hauer's exposition, Jung delivers his psychological commentary on Kundalini yoga: the chakras read as a ladder of consciousness, the serpent-fire as the perilous ascent of the impersonal within the personal. He warns the room like a mountain guide: these are not exercises for Europeans to imitate but a map by which to recognize where the psyche's weather is already carrying them. The East is admitted to the consulting room, on Swiss terms, with ropes.
suggested_refs: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga (1932 seminar notes)
sources: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga, ed. Shamdasani

stops.name: Berlin, the seminar in the darkening Reich
stops.campa: In the first summer of the new Reich Jung gives a week's seminar in Berlin on dreams, before an audience in which enthusiasm and dread sit in the same chairs. He has seen this weather before (in 1918 he wrote of the blond beast stirring in its underground prison), and he watches Wotan, the old wind-god of his mother's people, take possession of a nation as he once took a single dreaming woman. The years that follow will tangle his name in the storm; the register records the seminar, the warning, and the wind.

stops.name: Eranos, Ascona-Moscia, the round table below Monte Verità
stops.campa: On the terraced shore of Lake Maggiore at Moscia, below Monte Verità, the corpus's own hill of anarchists, dancers and sun-worshippers, Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn opens the first Eranos Tagung, the shared meal of the spirit, and Jung lectures on the process of individuation. Under the cedars, at the round table by the water, the learning of Europe and Asia sits down together each August: Corbin will bring the angel of Persia, Scholem the Kabbalah, Zimmer the gods of India, Kerényi the Greeks. For nearly two decades this garden is the capital of Jung's public thought: a Goethean colony on the Goethe atlas, facing south.
sources: Hans Thomas Hakl, Eranos: An Alternative Intellectual History

stops.name: Bombay, India entered
stops.campa: Invited by the British-Indian government to the jubilee of the Indian Science Congress, Jung lands at Bombay in December and India rises around him: a dreamlike world of temple crowds, ochre saints, and a civilization that never expelled the opposites. He resolves to travel it as he traveled Africa: not to convert or be converted, but to see Europe again from a great distance. He declines, throughout, to call on the holy men, wishing to owe his truth to no guru: a discourtesy he commits deliberately, and confesses in the canon.

stops.name: Sanchi, the hill of the stupas
stops.campa: At Sanchi, on the green hill where the great stupa has stood since Ashoka, an unexpected emotion seizes Jung with the force of possession: the stillness of the domes, the gates carved with the whole breathing world, the distant plain. Here Buddhism becomes real to him at a stroke: the Buddha understood as the self that outgrows the gods, the wheel set turning by a man. He walks the circumambulation path clockwise with the pilgrims, a Basel doctor pacing the oldest circle he has yet joined, and the hill accepts him.
suggested_refs: Great Stupa of Sanchi, north torana

stops.name: Konarak, the black pagoda
stops.campa: At Konarak on the Orissa shore Jung walks around the Black Pagoda, the fallen sun-temple built as the chariot of Surya, its wheels taller than men, its walls a surf of gods coupling in stone. His pandit explains, whispering, that the obscene sculptures are a means to spiritualization: the common man must be reminded of his dharma as flesh before he can be led beyond it. Jung, whose first dream was a phallus enthroned underground, receives the lecture with the composure of a man being shown his own childhood by strangers. The sun-wheel and the man-eater are one temple here, above ground, unashamed.

stops.name: Calcutta, the fever
stops.campa: At Calcutta, garlanded with the honorary doctorates of Allahabad, Benares and Calcutta (Islam, Hinduism and British-Indian medicine in three hoods), Jung is felled by dysentery and lies ten days in the English hospital. The fever is India's last argument: the subcontinent, he says later, was becoming too much, and the illness a device to remove him from the flood of impressions into a white room. In the enforced stillness the psyche prepares its verdict on the whole journey, and delivers it as only it delivers anything: as a dream.

stops.name: Calcutta, the dream of the Grail refused to the subcontinent
stops.campa: Convalescent in the hospital, Jung dreams himself with his friends on an unknown island off the south coast of England, where in a dark castle the celebration of the Grail is to be held tonight, but the Grail is not yet there, and he must swim the cold channel alone to fetch it. Imperiously the dream wipes India from him: not for him the wisdom of the yogis; his task lies with the neglected Grail of the West, the unhealed Christian vessel. He rises homeward bound and never leaves the ship at the ports of return, reading Grail texts in his cabin the whole way.
stops.quote: Imperiously, the dream wiped away all the intense impressions of India and swept me back to the too-long-neglected concerns of the Occident, which had formerly been expressed in the quest for the Holy Grail.
suggested_refs: Emma Jung, The Grail Legend (her lifework)

stops.name: Kandy, the drums of the Tooth, and home
stops.campa: In the hill temple at Kandy, before the relic of the Buddha's tooth, Jung hears the evening drummers in the mandapam play the drum-language of sacrifice: young men drumming to the young Buddha as the Elgonyi breathed to the young sun. Ceylon he receives as the antechamber of paradise and the end of the eastern road. Then the ship, the cabin, the Grail books; India astern like a great dream one honours by not imitating. He carries home the black pagoda, the stupa hill, and the refusal: the freight of a man sent back to finish his own religion.
suggested_refs: Temple of the Tooth, Kandy drummers

segments.name: Visions: The Stone and the Lightning

stops.name: Zurich, the clinic, the earth seen from a thousand miles
stops.campa: A broken foot, then an infarct, and Jung hangs at the edge of death while the nurse sees him wrapped in a bright glow. He floats a thousand miles above the earth and sees it whole: Ceylon beneath his feet, India, Arabia, the Himalayan snows, the globe bathed in gloriously blue light. Near him hangs a huge dark block of stone, a temple hollowed like those of the Kandy lake, its entrance lit with little flames; and as he approaches, the earthly husk of him (Küsnacht, books, opinions) burns away like painted cloth. He is about to enter and meet all that he ever was.
stops.quote: It seemed to me that I was high up in space. Far below I saw the globe of the earth, bathed in a gloriously blue light.

stops.name: Zurich, the clinic, the doctor in his primal form
stops.campa: At the threshold of the stone temple the image of Dr. Haemmerli floats up from Europe, framed in a golden laurel chain, the basileus of Kos, the healer in his primal form, bearing the protest of the earth: Jung has no right to leave, thirty women are waiting. The vision breaks; Jung returns to life resentfully, and with dread for the doctor, who has appeared in the archetype and must therefore die. On the fourth of April Jung sits up on the edge of his bed for the first time; the same day Haemmerli takes to his own bed and never leaves it. The exchange is exact.
stops.quote: On April 4, 1944 — I still remember the exact date — I was allowed to sit up on the edge of my bed for the first time since the beginning of my illness, and on this same day the doctor took to his bed and did not leave it again... I was his last patient.

stops.name: Bollingen, the cube stone carved
stops.campa: For his seventy-fifth year the quarry sends Bollingen a wrongly measured cube of stone; the mason would return it, but Jung claims the error: this is my stone. On one face he carves the little hooded Telesphoros with his lantern, the manikin of the attic beam come home after sixty-five years, circled by Greek: 'Time is a child, playing like a child... To the roaming Telesphoros, who shines out of the depths.' On another, the alchemists' orphan speaks in Latin. The stone stands outside the tower, facing the lake, explaining the tower to anyone who can read.
stops.quote: I am an orphan, alone; nevertheless I am found everywhere. I am one, but opposed to myself. I am youth and old man at one and the same time.
stops.quote_source: Inscription carved by Jung on the Bollingen stone; Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 8

stops.name: Küsnacht, Answer to Job: the fear of God written
stops.campa: In the fevers of an illness, in a single burning draft, Jung writes Answer to Job: the case of the man of Uz reopened, Yahweh examined and found less conscious than his creature, the incarnation read as God's own answer to Job's moral victory, and the pastor's son of Klein-Hüningen at last answering his father's broken faith with a theology of terrifying honesty. He knows the book will bring the roof down on him, clergy and colleagues in one chorus, and he publishes it anyway, being now old enough, he says, to owe the truth this last debt.
stops.quote: If there is anything like the spirit seizing one by the scruff of the neck, it was the way this book came into being.
stops.quote_source: Jung, letter on the writing of Answer to Job (1951)

stops.name: Eranos, the last lecture: synchronicity named in public
stops.campa: At the Eranos Tagung of 1951 Jung mounts the terrace lectern above Lake Maggiore for the last time and gives the garden his final gift: 'On Synchronicity', the acausal connecting principle, the meaningful coincidence raised to a pillar of the world beside space, time and causality; the scarab at the window and the golden castle from Frankfurt given their law. The round table that heard the archetypes named now hears causality itself demoted. The old man descends from the hill of the Goethe atlas and does not lecture there again; the cedars keep the echo.

stops.name: Küsnacht, Emma dies: the queen
stops.campa: Emma Jung dies at Küsnacht on 27 November, fifty-two years and nine months after the wedding above the falls: analyst in her own right, mistress of the Grail legend she had worked at for thirty years: the western quest her husband's India dream assigned to their house. At the funeral the old man stands and is heard saying it over and over: she was a queen, she was a queen. Of the foundation of the house, the canon speaks plainly; what remains at Seestrasse 228 is a king in winter and the god over the door, called and present.
stops.quote: She was a queen! She was a queen!
stops.quote_source: Jung at Emma's funeral, as recorded in Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and Work
sources: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and Work

stops.name: Bollingen, the stone for Emma; the tower completed
stops.campa: In his grief Jung works stone. He cuts a memorial tablet for Emma with the words a knight would set for his lady: O vessel, sign of devotion and obedience, and beside it tablets for the ancestors of the House of Jung, the Basel doctor, the legend-line of Goethe, carved with arms and names, the genealogy the chain now carries set first in Bollingen stone. And after her death he adds the upper storey to the tower, the part that had always been withheld: it represents himself, he says, the ego-personality completed late. The building and the builder finish together.
stops.quote: After my wife's death... I suddenly realized that the small central section which crouched so low and hidden was myself! I could no longer hide myself behind the 'maternal' and the 'spiritual' towers.
sources: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and Work

stops.name: Küsnacht, Memories, Dreams, Reflections begun
stops.campa: In his eighty-second spring Jung sits down with Aniela Jaffé and begins to tell his life, and soon takes the pen himself for the first chapters, the parsonage, the falls, the man-eater on the throne, writing his childhood with a child's terrible candor. He will call the book the report of his personal myth: outward events have faded, he says; only the inner experiences have kept their color. The canon of this whole itinerary is being composed at this stop: the traveler, still traveling, turns and draws the map.
stops.quote: My life is a story of the self-realization of the unconscious.

stops.name: Küsnacht, Serrano received: the letter to the south
stops.campa: Miguel Serrano, the Chilean pilgrim of Montagnola and the Himalayas, comes to Seestrasse 228 in May from Hermann Hesse's door, and the old man receives him in the upstairs study among the alchemy books. They speak of the Self, of Shiva and the circle, of the coming man. The friendship runs on in letters; the letter of 14 September 1960, which the corpus itself carries inscribed, sets down Jung's late testament on consciousness and the creative daimon; and Serrano will stand at the gate again in the last May of Jung's life. The south has sent its witness, and the witness will write the record of two friendships.
suggested_refs: Miguel Serrano, C.G. Jung and Hermann Hesse: A Record of Two Friendships
sources: Miguel Serrano, C.G. Jung and Hermann Hesse

stops.name: Küsnacht, the BBC at the door: I know
stops.campa: John Freeman's Face to Face cameras are set up in the Küsnacht study, and on 22 October the interview goes out to the English world. Freeman asks the boy of the Basel cathedral square, now eighty-four: do you now believe in God? The pause is long, the smile longer. 'Difficult to answer,' says Jung. 'I know. I don't need to believe. I know.' Letters descend on the BBC like the postbag of a prophet. Sixty years of empiricism compressed into four words: the pastor's son has answered his father's pulpit at last, on television.
stops.quote: I don't need to believe. I know.
stops.quote_source: Face to Face, BBC, broadcast 22 October 1959

stops.name: Küsnacht, the dream of the marketplace: the last book commanded
stops.campa: Asked to write for the general public, Freeman and the publishers pressing, Jung refuses: he is old and tired, and has never written for the crowd. Then he dreams: he stands in a public square and speaks, not to doctors, but to a multitude of ordinary people who listen and understand him. The unconscious has countermanded the refusal, and Jung obeys it as he has obeyed it since the man-eater's throne: he accepts Man and His Symbols, gathers his heirs to write it with him, and works on his own chapter to within days of the end. The last labor is assigned by dream, like the first terror.

stops.name: Küsnacht, the last dream: the tree of gold and the stone of wholeness
stops.campa: In the last days, after a stroke, tended by Ruth Bailey, the fourth foretold on the Africa boat, keeping the last camp, Jung dreams the closing dream of the canon: a great round stone on a high plateau, hewn and whole, and at its foot the engraved words of the sign; and a square of trees whose roots reach around the earth and envelop him, and among the roots gold threads are gleaming. The stone of Klein-Hüningen, the cube of Bollingen, the temple block in orbit: all one stone now, inscribed and finished. He tells the dream; the household writes it down; the work is sealed.
stops.quote: And this shall be a sign unto you of Wholeness and Oneness.
stops.quote_source: Jung's last dream, told to Ruth Bailey; recorded in Marie-Louise von Franz, C. G. Jung: His Myth in Our Time
sources: Marie-Louise von Franz, C. G. Jung: His Myth in Our Time

stops.name: Küsnacht, 6 June 1961: the lightning splits the poplar
stops.campa: At Seestrasse 228, in the house under the sentence of the ever-present god, Carl Gustav Jung dies quietly in the late afternoon of 6 June, his family about him. As he goes, a storm breaks over the lake, and lightning strikes the tall poplar in the garden, the tree he sat beneath, splitting its trunk and strewing the lawn with bark; the household keeps the event as canon. Far off at sea, van der Post, homeward from Africa, sees him on a white mountain, waving. The falls at Laufen keep roaring. The journey from parsonage to parsonage-of-his-own is complete: called and not called, the god was present.
stops.quote: I'll be seeing you.
stops.quote_source: Jung's words in Laurens van der Post's vision at sea at the hour of death; van der Post, Jung and the Story of Our Time
sources: Laurens van der Post, Jung and the Story of Our Time
Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and Work
